newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African court hears that Botha ordered bombing.
newsitem.headline: S.African court hears that Botha ordered bombing.

text.p: Former South African president P.W. Botha was dragged deeper on Tuesday into accusations that he knew a great deal about the apartheid regime's dirty tricks against opponents -- and even ordered a civilian bombing.

Convicted state assassin Eugene de Kock said in a Pretoria court his superiors had told him Botha had directly ordered the bombing of the Johannesburg headquarters of the black trade union federation Cosatu in 1987.

The former death squad leader de Kock, testifying in the hope of winning leniency for the six murders and scores of other charges he was convicted of last month, said he had asked his security boss at the time who ordered the Cosatu House bombing.
"From the highest was the reply and I said 'from where, the state president?' and he said 'yes'," he told the court.

De Kock, with square-rimmed glasses and wearing a grey suit, also admitted he was in a South African group that flew to London in March 1982 to blow up the headquarters of Nelson Mandela's exiled African National Congress (ANC).
Suspicious Heathrow airport police had interrogated him for five hours but let him go, and when the explosives went off he was relaxing on a flight home.

On Monday de Kock said Botha, who yielded to reformer F.W. de Klerk in 1989, must have known about a South African agents' attack he led into neighbouring Lesotho on suspected ANC members in which some 10 people died in 1985.
"I have no doubt state president P.W. Botha knew about it," he told the hushed court, where even ANC cabinet ministers have come to hear his revelations.
Botha has remained silent on these and earlier accusations, saying simply he has nothing to apologise for. He could not be reached for comment on Tuesday.
De Kock, hoping to escape a life sentence, has vowed to name his superiors in the highest ranks in order to prove that the crimes he committed were done according to orders.
So far he has named apartheid-era foreign minister Pik Botha, police chief Adriaan Vlok and numerous security generals as figures who must have known about the cross-border raids.

He also named a senior white Inkatha Freedom Party official, Phillip Powell, as his contact in the Zulu-based party for the training and equipping of Inkatha members in order to counter the ANC and Pan Africanist Congress (PAC) liberation movements.
Asked about his relationship with Inkatha, de Kock replied: "It was not a blood link. There was a common enemy: the PAC and the ANC."

P.W. Botha, who says he started the reforms that under de Klerk led to black majority rule in 1994 after three centuries of white supremacy, is now a frail 80-year-old and lives quietly with his wife at a retirement home by the sea.

De Klerk blamed the state of emergency Botha imposed in the 1980s for creating an atmosphere ripe for many of the human rights abuses that retired archbishop Desmond Tutu's Truth and Reconciliation Commission is trying to exorcise.
De Kock, 47, has applied to the commission for an amnesty. This will depend partly on how frank he is in telling the secrets he knows.
